reader.title: Killing of Bill Mulcahy, Jack Kingsbury and Nevada Jim
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A private party of twelve or fifteen men from Calabasas pursued three men accused of murder into Sonora and killed two in a gunfight; the third, wounded and held for hanging, shot himself (A3, A11, A13, A28).

A party of private men described as 'vigilantes' with no reported legal authority hunted down accused murderers, killed two, and were preparing a rope to hang the captured third when he shot himself (A13, A18, A28); the two deaths came in an exchange of fire the fugitives opened (A11, A28), so the killing was closer to a posse fight than an execution, and no paper identifies any of the dead as Black.

Independent local Arizona reports (Tombstone Epitaph and Independent) and the separate Albuquerque and Prescott wires agree that a pursuing party overtook and killed the three men (A1, A3, A11, A12, A28), though they differ on numbers, casualties, date and how Nevada Jim died.

summary.text: The killing of Bill Mulcahy, Jack Kingsbury and Nevada Jim took place in Sonora, Mexico, in July 1882, when a party of armed men from Calabasas, Arizona Territory, pursued the three across the border and killed them.
Mulcahy and Kingsbury were shot dead in a gunfight, and Nevada Jim, wounded and held while a rope was found to hang him, shot one of his captors and then himself.
Wire services carried the story nationally as the work of "Arizona vigilantes", with a closing note that local citizens approved.

According to an informant of the Tombstone Epitaph, on Sunday evening, July 9, four railroaders, James Moroney, Mulcahy, Kingsbury and Nevada Jim, quarreled over a woman at a Mexican camp near Igo's ranch, about twelve miles from Calabasas, and Moroney was shot in the forehead.

The other three went on to a dance hall in Calabasas, where friends of Moroney found them and opened fire; nearly everyone in the room joined in, leaving two men dead, a Mexican likely dying, and four men and three women wounded.
The three escaped through the tent toward Sonora, and twelve men "armed to the teeth" set out after them at dusk.
Later wire versions summarized the accusation differently, saying the three had killed two Mexicans and wounded two Americans at Calabazas.

The Albuquerque dispatch, sent as a special to the Cincinnati Enquirer, said a party of fifteen kept up the pursuit through a Monday and sighted the fugitives at 4 p.m. heading on tired horses for a rocky peak.
The three fired on the approaching riders from the rocks with Winchesters and wounded a man named Hennessy in the shoulder; the pursuers then dismounted, advanced under cover and rushed the position.
Two of the fugitives were quickly killed and Nevada Jim was shot through the thighs.

In this account the party "spared his life until a rope could be produced to hang him", but he seized a dead comrade's revolver, shot a vigilante named Fallehy through the lung, and then shot himself in the head.
A shorter digest said he had been told to prepare for immediate death.

The Tombstone Independent, quoted by the Arizona Weekly Citizen, placed the fight among scattered rocks on an open plain seventy-five or eighty miles over the border and said all three were killed in it.
The bodies were left where they fell, and the party returned to Calabasas, where, the Independent said, it was warmly greeted.
No report of an inquest, arrest or other legal action concerning the pursuers appears in the coverage.
The first word came in a Tombstone dispatch of July 13-14, printed from Sacramento to Washington, that three "desperadoes" had been killed in Sonora by a pursuing party.
A Calabasas-datelined version in the Benton Weekly Record reported only two killed.
From July 21 brief Albuquerque and Prescott wires spread the names, under heads such as "Short Work With Outlaws" and "Vigilantes at Work".

The longer Albuquerque story, headed "HE LAUGHED LAST" in the Memphis Public Ledger, cast the pursuers as "avengers" and the fugitives as "cutthroats", and ended with the line that "The citizens generally approved of the vigilants course."
Weekly papers in the Midwest and East reprinted it through early August, several placing Calabazas in New Mexico.
The Chicago Illinois Staats-Zeitung, citing the Colorado Journal, presented the case as Judge Lynch's quick justice in New Mexico.
Closer to home, the Epitaph treated Calabasas with irony as "HELL'S HOLLOW", and a Cincinnati Times-Star feature reprinted in New York used the dance-hall shooting to lampoon the town.
No paper in the coverage identifies any of the men as Black.

The accounts differ on the size of the party (twelve or fifteen), on the date, which the Tombstone dispatch places before July 14 and a wire variant on the 17th, and on the pursuers' losses, which range from one man wounded to two killed.

The local Independent account does not mention Nevada Jim's capture or suicide, and the Epitaph's account of the dance hall, where the pursuers fired first, differs from wire versions that blame the three for the deaths there.

accounts.label: Tombstone Epitaph informant
accounts.gist: Moroney was shot in a quarrel over a woman near Igo's ranch; his friends fired into a Calabasas dance hall where the three were dancing, a melee left two dead and seven wounded, and twelve men rode after the escaped three toward Sonora.

accounts.label: Tombstone Independent
accounts.gist: The pursuers overtook the three 75-80 miles over the border, killed all three in a fight among rocks, had two or three men severely wounded, and left the dead on the ground.

accounts.label: Albuquerque wire (Cincinnati Enquirer special)
accounts.gist: Fifteen pursuers cornered the three at a rocky peak on a Monday afternoon; two were killed, Nevada Jim was wounded and held for hanging, then shot Fallehy and himself.

accounts.label: Variant wire digest
accounts.gist: Twelve pursuers, fight on the 17th, one vigilante killed at the first volley and Folley shot dead by Nevada Jim.

accounts.label: Colorado Journal (German translation)
accounts.gist: The wounded Hennessey charged back alone and shot two of the men through the heart before Nevada Jim was taken and killed himself.

framing.detail: The Albuquerque wire called the pursuers 'avengers' and the fugitives 'cutthroats' and 'villains', and closed that citizens generally approved the vigilantes' course.
The Tombstone Epitaph treated Calabasas ironically as 'HELL'S HOLLOW' and a 'sinful hollow', mocking both the drinking railroaders and the town.
Eastern and Midwestern papers carried short digests under heads such as 'Short Work With Outlaws' and 'Three Desperadoes Killed'.

record_check.dossier: No paper states the race of the three; the Epitaph calls them railroaders and they are set against 'Mexicans' in the wire. Nothing marks them as Black.
Pursuit from Calabasas, Arizona Territory; killed 75-80 miles inside Sonora, Mexico.
Between about July 10 and July 17, 1882; the triggering killings were Sunday, July 9.
A party of 12-15 Calabasas men, friends of the slain Moroney; members named Hennessy and Fallehy.
Pursuer casualties conflict: one to three wounded, or one or two killed; race of the pursuers not stated.

record_check.record: said to have murdered two Mexicans
record_check.dossier: Accused of killing James Moroney and of a part in the Calabasas dance-hall shooting; the 'two Mexicans' version is the wire's.

info: The fight is dated to a Monday at 4 p.m. by the Albuquerque wire, given as 'the 17th' in one variant; the Tombstone dispatch of July 13-14 already reported the three killed 'a few days ago', which would place it about July 10-13.

The three were overtaken some seventy-five or eighty miles over the border in Sonora, Mexico, at a rocky peak or a bunch of scattered rocks on an open plain; the triggering shootings were at Igo's ranch, about twelve miles from Calabasas, and in Calabasas, Arizona Territory.

Bill Mulcahy (also Mulcaby, Mulcahey, Muleahey; William in one digest), Jack (John) Kingsbury, and a man called Nevada Jim ('Nevada Bill' in one dispatch); the Epitaph calls them railroaders. No paper states their race.
Accused of killing James Moroney near Igo's ranch and of a part in the Calabasas dance-hall shooting; wire versions say they killed two Mexicans and wounded or mortally wounded two Americans.
A party organized at Calabasas, described as friends of the dead Moroney and as 'Arizona vigilantes'; two members are named Hennessy (Hennessey) and Fallehy ('Folley' in one variant).
All three pursued men died; the bodies were left where they fell and the party returned to Calabasas, where it was warmly greeted.
